_note: Plain meanings of court words, and who people are, for readers with no background. Shown on /glossary/ and, for the terms a page uses, in 'Words and people on this page' on each day. A term is matched by `match` (a regular expression, case-insensitive).

terms.plain: Ventura testified this was Combs's name for days-long sexual encounters he arranged with male sex workers and watched. Jane called similar encounters "hotel nights".
Jane's name for the encounters she testified Combs arranged with male sex workers in hotels.
One charge in the indictment. Combs faced five counts.
Count 1: agreeing with others to run a criminal enterprise through a pattern of crimes. The jury found Combs not guilty of it.
Counts 2 and 4: using force, threats, fraud or coercion to make a person take part in paid sex. The jury found Combs not guilty of both.

terms.term: Transportation to engage in prostitution (Mann Act)
terms.plain: Counts 3 and 5: arranging travel across state lines for people to take part in paid sex. The jury found Combs guilty of both.
The jury was not persuaded beyond a reasonable doubt. It is not a finding about what anyone lived through.
The standard of proof in a criminal trial. The prosecution must prove each charge to this standard; the defense does not have to prove anything.
A lawyer for the government who brings the case. AUSA means Assistant United States Attorney.
Questions from the side that called the witness.
Questions from the other side, testing the witness's account.
Follow-up questions: redirect from the side that called the witness, then re-cross from the other side.
A court order that lets a witness be made to testify; what they say on the stand cannot be used to charge them.
Using the constitutional right not to answer questions that could be used against oneself.
A deal to tell prosecutors what a person knows, with limits on how it can be used against them.
Ending a trial before a verdict and starting again. The defense asked for one twice; both requests were denied.
A defense request that the judge acquit because the evidence was not enough for a jury to convict. Denied in this case.
Removing a possible juror without giving a reason, during jury selection. Strikes may not be based on race.
A juror who hears the whole case and replaces a sitting juror if one has to leave.
An instruction urging a jury that says it is stuck to keep trying to reach a verdict.
A witness, often an agent or paralegal, who walks the jury through records such as phone data or flight logs.
A statement made outside court, offered to prove what it says. It is often not allowed.
Shown to the judge and jury but kept from the public.
An order limiting what people involved in a case may say publicly about it.
A second courtroom where the public and press watch the trial on video.
A non-disclosure agreement: a contract promising not to tell.
Homeland Security Investigations, the federal agency whose agents investigated the case.
A meeting of the judge and lawyers, without the jury, to settle the instructions the jury will be given.
A period after prison when a person is monitored by a probation officer and must follow conditions.
A name used in court instead of a witness's real name. "Mia" and "Jane" are pseudonyms; this site never shows anything that could identify them.
The federal judge who presided over the trial.
Combs's lead defense lawyer.
A Combs defense lawyer; she gave the defense's opening statement.
A Combs defense lawyer who questioned several witnesses, including Mia.
A Combs defense lawyer who argued legal motions.
A Combs defense lawyer who questioned Bryana Bongolan.
A Combs defense lawyer.
A federal prosecutor on the case.
A federal prosecutor; she gave the prosecution's opening statement.
A federal prosecutor; she gave the prosecution's closing argument.
A federal prosecutor on the case.
Cassie Ventura's husband.
Combs's chief of staff. She was not charged and did not testify.
